"Toward Scalable Terminal Task Synthesis via Skill Graphs"
Terminal-agent training needs more diverse workflows.
This Tencent Hunyuan paper, SkillSynth, builds a graph of terminal scenarios and skills, samples paths through it, then turns those paths into executable tasks.
It controls the skill/state transitions agents practice, not just the number of tasks, which leads to better terminal-agent training and stronger Terminal-Bench results.

"Model Spec Midtraining: Improving How Alignment Training Generalizes"
A lot of alignment training teaches models what to say, but not why those behaviors are right.
So before normal alignment fine-tuning, this research trains the model on synthetic documents that discuss its Model Spec, including its values, rules, and reasoning, then do the usual supervised alignment.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)

“GLM-5V-Turbo: Toward a Native Foundation Model for Multimodal Agents”
Most multimodal agents today are still basically text agents with vision adapters, and a lot of reasoning failures are actually the model failing to see the interface, layout, chart, or object correctly.
GLM-5V-Turbo is built around the idea that perception should be part of the core reasoning loop, not just an input adapter.
In this model, they added a new vision encoder (CogViT) for stronger fine-grained perception, with multimodal multi-token prediction so image+text training stays efficient.
It was jointly trained/RL across 30+ task categories spanning perception, reasoning, coding, GUI use, and tool use, with a broader multimodal toolchain plus integration with external agent frameworks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHvOG1tWQAED0Le.png

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"DGPO: Distribution Guided Policy Optimization for Fine Grained Credit Assignment"
RL for reasoning has a credit assignment problem. One reward basically gets spread across the whole chain-of-thought.
This paper, DGPO, fixes that by turning policy deviation into a token-level guidance signal.
Instead of using an unstable KL penalty that punishes novel reasoning paths, it uses bounded Hellinger distance + entropy gating. This lets the model push harder on the steps that likely caused success, while down weighting boilerplate and hallucinated detours.
This gives finer process supervision without needing a critic.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHvONwTXgAEwife.png

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Representational Curvature Modulates Behavioral Uncertainty in LLMs"
Most interpretability work studies what features live inside LLMs.
But this paper studies something deeper, which is the geometry of the whole evolving representation.
The key result is that representational curvature modulates behavioral uncertainty.
If the model’s internal trajectory over recent tokens is straighter, the next token is easier to predict and entropy is lower. If the trajectory bends, uncertainty rises.
They also show this geometry is not decorative too. It emerges over training, trajectory-aligned edits causally change entropy, and straightness regularization can modestly improve confidence without hurting loss.
This turns model uncertainty from just an output statistic into a geometric property of the computation itself.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HH0ApU8WcAcSe5e.png

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Sparser, Faster, Lighter Transformer Language Models”
LLMs are naturally sparse in their feedforward layers, but unstructured sparsity usually doesn’t get you real speed on GPUs, because the hardware stack is built for dense compute.
The key idea of the paper is to redesign the sparse format and kernels around GPU execution, so FFN sparsity becomes practical instead of theoretical.
With mild L1 regularization, this paper got >99% sparsity with little quality loss, and with gains in speed, memory, and energy.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HH5tzQaXIAA5-7m.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Continuous Latent Diffusion Language Model”
Most diffusion language models still use diffusion to recover token-like states, just in a different generation order.
However, this paper uses diffusion in a different way. It learns a continuous latent prior for global semantics first, then decodes that latent into text.
It treats language modeling as planning meaning in latent space and only then realizing the wording, and they show that this can scale competitively up to 2000 EFLOPs against autoregressive models, especially for tasks needing deeper semantic planning.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HH5t-CfWoAIzkp_.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Demystifying Manifold Constraints in LLM Pre-training"
LLM pre-training depends on a stack of heuristic tricks, eg. normalization layers, weight decay, and optimizer tuning.
This paper suggests that by constraining weight matrices to geometric manifolds like spectral or Frobenius spheres reduces most of these heuristics.
They introduced this optimizer called MACRO, which is a single-loop Riemannian method with provable convergence that keeps weights on-manifold every step.
Manifold constraints bound activation scales, replacing learnable RMSNorm. Muon diverges without it but MACRO doesn't. They also lock the relative learning rate from step one, replacing weight decay entirely as ablations show it has zero effect.
On QWEN3-like models up to 1B, MACRO matches or edges out MuonH while maintaining strict geometric guarantees.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIABFJPXEAA5WyB.png

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Iterative Finetuning is Mostly Idempotent"
If a model has a behavioral tendency and you train the next generation on its outputs, does the tendency snowball? This paper actually finds that it's mostly no.
So they seed models with traits like sycophancy and misalignment, then repeatedly train new models on their predecessors' outputs across SFT, synthetic document finetuning, and DPO.
Under SFT and SDF, traits almost always decay or flatline. The rare cases of amplification are extremely brittle and come at the cost of coherence collapsing into emoji loops or repetitive fragments.
The one exception is continual DPO, where weights persist across cycles and traits reliably amplify. But reinitializing from the base model each cycle kills the effect, pointing to weight accumulation as the mechanism.
Limiting continual post-training is likely an effective prevention, and the amplification-coherence tradeoff acts as a natural ceiling on how far traits can drift.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIABXqQXkAE-vR8.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Manifold Steering Reveals the Shared Geometry of Neural Network Representation and Behavior"
Most activation steering treats concepts like directions, but model representations are often curved, so straight line steering can cut through unnatural internal states.
The key idea of the paper is to steer along the activation manifold instead of through it.
Across LLM reasoning tasks and a visual world model, manifold steering produced smoother and more natural behavior, while linear steering caused probability mass or visual states to jump abruptly.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIEKgoJXoAAO-ak.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Sharpness-Aware Pretraining Mitigates Catastrophic Forgetting”
Better base models don’t always become better fine-tuned models, because post-training can overwrite pretrained capabilities.
So this paper pretrain models into flatter loss regions, so later updates from fine-tuning or quantization cause less damage.
Using SAM, higher learning rates, and shorter annealing, this paper reduces forgetting by up to 80%, and at 1B scale cuts forgetting by 31% after fine-tuning and 40% after 4-bit quantization.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIEKtYVWkAEe2av.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“The Truth Lies Somewhere in the Middle of the Generated Tokens”
LLMs don’t store the meaning of a prompt in one hidden state. As they generate, the meaning gets spread across many token embeddings.
So this paper propose a mean-pool over generated token embeddings instead of using the last token or prompt tokens.
This creates stronger semantic embeddings because generation makes the model unpack the prompt into its own internal representation.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIJHnVlXMAAE_22.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Attention Drift: What Autoregressive Speculative Decoding Models Learn”
Speculative decoding makes LLM inference faster, but drafters break under small template changes and long context. But why?
This paper shows that as the drafter predicts more tokens, its attention drifts away from the prompt and onto its own recent guesses.
The key fix is to normalize the drafter’s hidden states so they stay stable across draft steps.
With post-norm and RMSNorm fusion, the paper gets up to 2x better acceptance under template perturbations and stronger long-context robustness.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIJHwXtXoAAfs-7.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“ELF: Embedded Language Flows”
Most diffusion LMs still treat language as discrete tokens, or keep forcing continuous states back into token space during generation.
This paper runs diffusion almost entirely in continuous embedding space, then convert to tokens only at the final step.
This makes language diffusion look much more like image diffusion, so tricks like Flow Matching, stochastic sampling, and classifier-free guidance become natural.
ELF beats strong discrete and continuous diffusion LMs with fewer sampling steps and about 10x fewer training tokens.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIN1n31WYAAx4MY.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Solve the Loop: Attractor Models for Language and Reasoning”
Looped Transformers can refine their thoughts internally, but they are usually unstable and tied to a fixed number of loops.
So this paper turned recurrence into a fixed-point problem, where a Transformer first makes an output-embedding guess, then an attractor module refines it until convergence.
This makes iterative reasoning trainable with constant memory, adaptive depth, and less compute.
The surprising part is equilibrium internalization because after training, the model learns to start near the fixed point, so the solver can almost disappear at inference.
In their experiment, a 770M Attractor Model beats a 1.3B Transformer trained on twice the tokens, and a 27M model gets 91.4% on Sudoku-Extreme and 93.1% on Maze-Hard.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIN1tuSWwAARcpW.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Efficient Pre-Training with Token Superposition”
LLM pretraining is bottlenecked by how many useful tokens you can consume per FLOP.
This paper temporarily merge nearby tokens into averaged embedding bags, train the model to predict the next bag, then switch back to normal next-token training.
This gives the model a cheap coarse pass over much more data without changing the final architecture, tokenizer, optimizer, or inference path.
At 10B A1B MoE scale, TST reaches better loss and evals with up to 2.5x less pretraining time at equal loss.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIVTi0fWsAAvi8M.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“δ-mem: Efficient Online Memory for Large Language Models”
LLMs need long-term memory, but extending context is expensive and often doesn’t mean the model actually uses the history well.
What this paper did is to store past information in a tiny 8x8 associative memory state, then use that state to make low-rank corrections inside attention.
So memory is not retrieved as text or added to the prompt. It directly steers the frozen model’s computation.
With only 4.87M trainable parameters, δ-mem improves Qwen3-4B from 46.79 to 51.66 average score, with bigger gains on memory-heavy benchmarks like MemoryAgentBench and LoCoMo.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIVToQIXQAAy2O_.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)

“Negation Neglect: When models fail to learn negations in training”
LLMs can understand a disclaimer in-context, but often fail to learn it during finetuning.
So when training on documents saying a claim is false can still implant the claim as true.
Qwen3.5 belief in fabricated claims rose from 2.5% to 88.6% after finetuning on documents full of warnings, almost the same as training on the false claims directly at 92.4%.
And more warnings did not fix it. Only local negation inside the claim, like Ed Sheeran did not win, mostly prevented the model from absorbing the story.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIYRrgoWEAAVQkD.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Self-Distilled Agentic RL”
Agent RL learns from sparse trajectory rewards, while self-distillation gives dense token guidance. But in multi-turn agents, naive distillation can break because privileged teacher signals get noisy as trajectories drift.
The key idea of this paper is to keep GRPO as the main optimizer and use a token-level gate to decide when self-distillation should matter.
This method trusts positive teacher signals more than negative ones, letting agents internalize retrieved skills without needing those skills at test time.
It improves GRPO by +9.4 on ALFWorld, +7.0 on Search-QA, and +10.2 on WebShop-Acc.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIZLIG4W8AEstqN.jpg

“VGGT-Ω”
3D reconstruction models is scaling like LLMs. Instead of relying on slow optimization pipelines, VGGT-Ω predicts cameras and depth in one feed-forward pass, even for dynamic video.
This research makes that scaling practical with scene registers, lighter prediction heads, 15x more supervised data, and 18M unlabeled videos.
This creates a much stronger spatial model, with big gains on static and dynamic reconstruction, and registers that transfer to robotics and language alignment.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIdsfihWIAAioof.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"SANA-WM Efficient Minute-Scale World Modeling"
Most world models can generate short controlled clips, but minute-long 720p rollouts usually need huge models, massive private data, and multi-GPU inference.
This paper makes long-horizon world modeling much more practical by combining frame-wise Gated DeltaNet with periodic softmax attention, plus dual-branch 6-DoF camera control for both global trajectory and fine motion.
SANA-WM trains on only 213K public pose-annotated clips, finishes in 15 days on 64 H100s, and can generate a 60s 720p controlled video on a single GPU, with a distilled version doing it in 34s on one RTX 5090.

summary:
“SlimQwen: Exploring the Pruning and Distillation in Large MoE Model Pre-training”
This new Qwen paper shows that pruning a pretrained MoE is much better than training the smaller MoE from scratch.
All you need to do is prune depth, width, and experts, preserve some experts while merging others, then recover with progressive distillation and multi-token prediction.
They compress Qwen3-Next-80A3B into a 23A2B model with competitive performance.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
Long-horizon reasoning is one of the largest obstacles in LLMs.
In our latest AI4Science talk, Sumeet (@sumeetrm) and Charlie (@CharlieLondon02) from Oxford discussed H1 and LongCoT, two projects focused on measuring and improving how models reason over long chains of steps.
Their H1 work shows that you can train these skills by composing short problems into longer chains, then using curriculum RL to gradually increase the horizon. LongCoT shows that frontier models are still very far from reliable long-horizon reasoning, with even the best models scoring below 10% on the main benchmark.
A really fascinating talk if you’re curious about why short reasoning benchmarks are no longer enough, and what it might take to make LLMs reliable on truly long tasks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIiwmF2W8AAr-jZ.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Extracting Search Trees from LLM Reasoning Traces Reveals Myopic Planning”
Reasoning models can write traces that look like real tree search, but this paper shows their decisions are mostly driven by shallow one-step evaluation.
They extract search trees from LLM CoT in four-in-a-row, then test whether deeper branches actually predict the final move.
The surprising result is that more search helps, but mainly through breadth, not depth. LLMs consider more candidate moves, yet largely ignore deeper lookahead when choosing. So CoT can look like planning without being the thing that makes the model plan.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIjZ7qPXcAAmzwg.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Steered LLM Activations are Non-Surjective"
Activation steering can make an LLM behave very differently, but that doesn't mean any prompt could have caused the same internal state.
This paper shows steering pushes activations off the prompt-reachable manifold into continuous-space holes that no discrete text input maps to.
So white-box control is not the same as black-box jailbreakability. Steering reveals what you can do with internal access, not necessarily what users can do with prompts.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIp-OGUWoAA2jeh.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Slicing and Dicing: Configuring Optimal MoE"
MoE models have a huge design space, but most choices are overcomplicated.
This paper runs 2,000+ pretraining runs up to 6.6B params and finds the key knobs are mostly expert count and expert granularity.
Adding more inactive experts keeps improving FLOP matched performance, while shared experts and heterogeneous experts do not really help.
The recipe is simple. Pick expert size for the active scale, then use memory on more experts. Dropless routing helps too.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIp-VtCWoAAXvg5.jpg

“RoPE Distinguishes Neither Positions Nor Tokens in Long Contexts”
RoPE is the default way LLMs track position, but this paper proves it breaks down as context gets long.
Attention becomes close to random at telling near from far, and can even assign the same score to different positions or different tokens.
Scaling the RoPE base only trades token confusion for position confusion, so longer context windows may need new positional mechanisms, not just bigger RoPE.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HIui5RYXsAEalSs.png

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Gated DeltaNet-2: a new linear attention model surpassing KDA and Mamba-3
summary:
New linear attention SoTA? Gated DeltaNet-2 from NVIDIA beats KDA and Mamba-3.
Prior DeltaNet/KDA models used one scalar gate for both erasing old memory and writing new memory.
This paper splits that into channel-wise erase and write gates, making memory edits more precise without losing efficient chunkwise training.
At 1.3B params on 100B tokens, it beats Mamba-2, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, and Mamba-3 variants, with the biggest gains on long-context retrieval.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJBZMx5XMAA-hIg.jpg
clean_summary:
New state-of-the-art linear attention model? Gated DeltaNet-2 from NVIDIA outperforms KDA and Mamba-3.

Previous DeltaNet and KDA models used a single scalar gate for both erasing old memory and writing new memory. This paper introduces a split into channel-wise erase and write gates, allowing more precise memory edits without sacrificing the efficiency of chunkwise training.

With 1.3 billion parameters trained on 100 billion tokens, Gated DeltaNet-2 beats Mamba-2, Gated DeltaNet, KDA, and Mamba-3 variants, especially improving long-context retrieval performance.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Tokenisation via Convex Relaxations"
Most LLM tokenizers still use BPE, a greedy merge algorithm that can waste vocab slots on locally good but globally suboptimal tokens.
This paper turns tokenizer training into a linear program, then rounds the solution into ConvexTok.
This gives a tokenizer with certifiable near optimality, within ~1% at common vocab sizes, plus better bits per byte and competitive downstream performance.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJBZSzOXkAAjZ9G.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)

summary:
"Imperfect World Models are Exploitable"
World models can look accurate, but still rank policies incorrectly, saying policy A is better than policy B when the real environment says the reverse.
This paper formalizes that failure as model exploitation and proves it is basically unavoidable for any nontrivial, nonequivalent world model on broad policy sets.
It also connects this to reward hacking and derives a safe horizon showing how model error compounds with planning depth.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJJBXIgWEAArOAH.jpg
clean_summary: World models can appear accurate but still rank policies incorrectly, indicating that policy A is better than policy B when the real environment says the opposite. This paper formalizes this failure as model exploitation and shows it is essentially unavoidable for any nontrivial, nonequivalent world model across broad policy sets. It also links this to reward hacking and derives a safe planning horizon that demonstrates how model error accumulates with increased planning depth.

summary:
"Vector Policy Optimization"
This paper trains models to generate diverse answer sets by using vector rewards, then randomly weighting reward dimensions so each answer can specialize in a different tradeoff.
Instead of optimizing one best response, VPO optimizes a set that covers the Pareto frontier.
On reasoning, tool use, navigation, and coding, VPO improves best@k and pass@k as the search budget grows, and even solves hard OpenEvolve problems GRPO cannot reach.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJNcg32WkAAhPNX.jpg
clean_summary:
Vector Policy Optimization trains models to generate diverse answer sets by using vector rewards and randomly weighting reward dimensions so each answer can specialize in different tradeoffs. Instead of optimizing for a single best response, VPO aims to cover the Pareto frontier, balancing multiple objectives.

On tasks involving reasoning, tool use, navigation, and coding, VPO improves metrics like best@k and pass@k as the search budget increases. It even solves challenging OpenEvolve problems that previous methods like GRPO cannot reach.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)

"PiD Fast and High-Resolution Latent Decoding with Pixel Diffusion"
Image models usually VAE decode first, then super-res later, which is slow and mostly reconstructs rather than creates detail.
This NVIDIA research makes the decoder itself a pixel diffusion model, so a 512^2 latent can directly become a 2048^2 or 4096^2 image.
With sigma-aware latent conditioning and 4-step distillation, PiD works across FLUX, SD3, DINOv2, and SigLIP latents, hitting about 210 ms for 2K decoding while beating cascaded SR quality.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Looped transformers with residual ODE treatment enable inference-time reuse of frozen checkpoints
summary:
Another cool research on Looped Transformers
They ask the question: "Can we loop a frozen, off-the-shelf checkpoint directly at inference time without any modifications?"
So naive repetition pushes hidden states outside the distribution later layers expect, so performance drops.
But if you treat transformer layers as Euler steps in a residual ODE and replaces naive loops with damped Runge–Kutta substeps, it is possible.
This lets the frozen models get extra latent compute at test time with no fine-tuning, no new weights, and no architecture changes.
And the best gains show up on hard knowledge MC tasks like MMLU-Pro, GPQA, and ARC.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJSGni_WMAg6qOE.jpg
clean_summary: Another interesting research on Looped Transformers explores whether a frozen, off-the-shelf checkpoint can be directly reused at inference time without modifications. Naive repetition of layers causes hidden states to drift outside the distribution expected by later layers, reducing performance. The solution models transformer layers as Euler steps in a residual ODE and replaces naive loops with damped Runge–Kutta substeps, allowing the frozen models to perform extra latent computation at test time without fine-tuning, new weights, or architecture changes. The biggest improvements are seen on challenging knowledge multiple-choice tasks like MMLU-Pro, GPQA, and ARC.

MaxRL shows that standard RL only optimizes a lower order approximation of the true maximum likelihood objective. The authors fix this with a single change to the advantage: divide by the group mean instead of the standard deviation, concentrating more learning signal on hard problems.
The result is up to 20x test-time scaling efficiency gains over GRPO, with substantially less pass@k degradation as training progresses.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"DiffusionBlocks: Block-wise Neural Network Training via Diffusion Interpretation"
End to end backprop stores activations through every layer, which is why deep Transformers is expensive to train.
This paper reinterprets residual blocks as diffusion denoising steps, so each block trains independently on its own noise range.
Only one block needs gradients at a time, giving roughly Bx memory savings while matching end to end training across ViTs, DiTs, diffusion LMs, AR Transformers, and recurrent depth models.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJWjBZJXUAwL_nS.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Large models can outperform filtered web data with no filtering
summary:
“A Bitter Lesson for Data Filtering”
A common consensus is that LLMs need carefully filtered web data, because noisy data can easily hurts in small compute regimes.
But this paper shows that with a large enough model size and training, the best filter is no filter.
Raw Common Crawl eventually beats RefinedWeb, DCLM-Baseline, and other filters, and large models can even benefit from shuffled low-quality data.
Data filtering may be another bitter lesson, where human curation wins early but loses to scale.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJWjP7aXAAM3VWD.jpg
clean_summary: A common belief is that LLMs require carefully filtered web data because noisy data can hurt performance, especially with small compute. However, this work shows that with sufficiently large models and training, using raw data like Common Crawl without filtering can outperform curated datasets like RefinedWeb and DCLM-Baseline. Large models can even benefit from shuffled low-quality data, suggesting that human curation may be advantageous early on but becomes less important as scale increases. The practical lesson is that scaling can reduce the need for data filtering.

clean_title: When does LeJEPA learn a world model?
summary:
New paper from Yann LeCun!
"When Does LeJEPA Learn a World Model?"
This paper proves that under Gaussian latent dynamics, LeJEPA can recover the hidden state behind nonlinear observations up to rotation.
The intuition is that linear latent features are the most stable across nearby views, while nonlinear features decay faster, so the objective naturally selects the real world variables.
The key caveat is that this guarantee holds under specific assumptions, and Gaussian latents are the unique case that guarantees this.

Quoting @SakanaAILabs
Introducing DiffusionBlocks: Block-wise Neural Network Training via Diffusion Interpretation
What if we didn’t have to hold an entire neural network in memory to train it?
Standard neural net training optimizes all parameters jointly. As a result, the memory required during training grows linearly with the depth of the network.
In our #ICLR2026 paper, we propose DiffusionBlocks, a principled framework to train networks one block at a time, drastically reducing memory requirements while matching end-to-end performance.
With DiffusionBlocks, we split the network into blocks and train them one at a time, so you only need memory for a single block.
How? We explicitly assign each block a role: to move the representation a little closer to the target than the block before it did. That role turns out to be precisely what a diffusion model does, step by step. Each block only needs to optimize its own objective and can be trained independently.
We validated this across five different architectures:
• ViT
• DiT
• Masked diffusion
• Autoregressive transformers
• Recurrent-depth transformers
In each case, performance is competitive with end-to-end training while using a fraction of the memory.
This perspective also extends naturally to recurrent-depth (Looped) transformers, which apply the same network iteratively and normally require expensive backpropagation through time (BPTT). Viewed through DiffusionBlocks, we can replace those multiple iterations with a single forward pass during training.
Read our paper and code, to learn more.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Parallax: scalable local linear attention for language modeling
summary:
"Parallax: Parameterized Local Linear Attention for Language Modeling"
Softmax attention acts like a local constant estimator over KV memory. Local Linear Attention is stronger, but too unstable and expensive to pretrain.
So Parallax makes it scalable by learning a query-like probe into KV covariance, adding a local linear correction without the per-token solver.
This gives better perplexity and downstream accuracy at 0.6B and 1.7B, with speed competitive with FlashAttention.
A surprising part is optimizer codesign. Because with Muon, the correction branch becomes high-rank, and useful. With AdamW, it mostly collapses.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJmEfiaXwAIEVHi.jpg
clean_summary: Parallax introduces a scalable local linear attention method for language modeling. Traditional softmax attention acts as a local constant estimator, while local linear attention is more powerful but unstable and costly to pretrain. Parallax learns a query-like probe into key-value covariance, adding a local linear correction without requiring a per-token solver. This approach improves perplexity and downstream accuracy on models of 0.6B and 1.7B parameters, with speed comparable to FlashAttention. An interesting finding is that optimizer choice affects the correction branch: with Muon, it becomes high-rank and useful, but with AdamW, it mostly collapses.

summary:
"Learn from your own latents, not tokens: A Sample Complexity Theory"
This paper explains why data2vec and JEPA can learn with much less data.
They showed that when data has hidden hierarchy, token prediction becomes harder as the hierarchy gets deeper. But latent prediction keeps the learning problem simple at every level.
Which suggests that models may learn faster when they stop predicting raw tokens and start predicting their own abstractions.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJmElimWoAEupX-.jpg

It shows that when data has a hidden hierarchy, predicting raw tokens becomes harder as the hierarchy deepens. However, predicting latent representations keeps the learning problem simple at every level. This suggests that models may learn faster when they focus on predicting their own abstractions instead of raw tokens.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: LoopMDM: Reusing Transformer Layers for Efficient Diffusion Language Models
summary:
"Looped Diffusion Language Models"
This paper LoopMDM simply reuses a few early-middle Transformer layers multiple times during denoising. It adds iterative thinking at the same parameter count, and lets the model spend more compute at inference by increasing the loop count.
The result is surprisingly good. It matches same-size masked diffusion models with up to 3.3x fewer training FLOPs, improves GSM8K by up to 8.5 points, and beats deeper non-looped models with similar compute.
The reason why it works is that masked tokens kinda act like a workspace, so looping lets them interact and revise each other before the model commits to an answer.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJsU4vwW0AEmcPM.jpg
clean_summary: LoopMDM reuses a few early-middle Transformer layers multiple times during denoising, adding iterative reasoning at the same parameter count. This approach allows the model to spend more compute at inference by increasing the loop count. The results are impressive: it matches the performance of similarly sized masked diffusion models with up to 3.3 times fewer training FLOPs, improves GSM8K accuracy by up to 8.5 points, and outperforms deeper non-looped models with comparable compute. The key insight is that masked tokens act like a workspace, and looping enables them to interact and revise each other before the model produces an answer.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Recursive flow matching for fast and stable physics forecasting
summary:
"Recursive Flow Matching"
Recursive Flow Matching makes physics forecasting much faster without losing accuracy.
So most diffusion models need many steps to simulate systems like fluids, climate, or wave dynamics. While vanilla flow matching is faster, it still often breaks down when forced into 1 or 2 steps.
So this paper fixes this by training the model on multiple rescaled flow paths that meet at the same state, then making those paths agree.
Which makes the learned trajectory smoother and more stable, so the model can generate accurate rollouts in just 1 or 2 steps.
It gets up to 20x faster inference than diffusion-based emulators and over 15% lower MSE than vanilla flow matching.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJsVGAeWMAAb09O.jpg
clean_summary: Recursive Flow Matching makes physics forecasting much faster without losing accuracy. Most diffusion models require many steps to simulate systems like fluids, climate, or wave dynamics. While vanilla flow matching is faster, it often fails when limited to 1 or 2 steps. This approach trains the model on multiple rescaled flow paths that meet at the same state and makes those paths agree, resulting in smoother and more stable trajectories. As a result, the model can generate accurate rollouts in just 1 or 2 steps, achieving up to 20 times faster inference than diffusion-based emulators and over 15% lower mean squared error than vanilla flow matching.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Why Larger Models Learn More"
This paper from Goodfire shows that scaling model size helps models remember the long tail.
Small models mostly spend their capacity on common and easy patterns, and when rare tasks appear, they do learn a bit, but the frequent-task updates overwrite it.
On the other hand, bigger models have enough capacity to fit common tasks without constant interference, so rare-task signals survive and accumulate.
They show this in toy models and OLMo from 4M to 4B params. So bigger models learn rarer tasks, store more task features, and suffer less gradient interference.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJvwx33X0AEkfj1.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Self Improving Language Models with Bidirectional Evolutionary Search"
Most LLM search still works by sampling more rollouts or extending one path at a time.
This paper's bidirectional evolutionary search does it in a smarter way.
It breaks the task backward into smaller verifiable goals, while evolving solutions forward by mixing useful parts from different attempts.
This lets the model find answers that normal sampling and tree search are unlikely to reach.
The gives better post-training and stronger test-time search on hard reasoning and open problem solving tasks.

clean_title: VLM^3: vision-language models as native 3D learners
summary:
"VLM^3: VLMs Are Native 3D Learners"
This paper shows that VLMs can learn 3D natively.
Most 3D vision systems rely on expert architectures, regression heads, heavy augmentations, and task-specific losses.
But they show that you can skip the majority of these designs.
All they did is unify focal length, reference pixels with normalized text coordinates, and scale the right data mixture.
A 4B VLM learns depth, object 3D reasoning, pixel correspondence, and camera pose with standard text training.
Depth goes from 0.84 to 0.90, and camera pose AUC jumps from 5 to 94.
So 3D may not need a separate expert model stack. It may just need the right interface for VLMs.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HJ2JN06X0AAhUKt.jpg
clean_summary: VLM^3 demonstrates that vision-language models (VLMs) can learn 3D understanding directly from standard text training, without relying on specialized architectures, regression heads, heavy augmentations, or task-specific losses. By unifying focal length, reference pixels, normalized text coordinates, and scaling the data mixture, a 4-billion-parameter VLM can acquire depth, object 3D reasoning, pixel correspondence, and camera pose estimation. The depth prediction accuracy improves from 0.84 to 0.90, and camera pose AUC jumps from 5 to 94, suggesting that effective 3D understanding may be achieved through the right interface for VLMs rather than separate expert models.

summary:
"Benchmarking Visual State Tracking in Multimodal Video Understanding"
A new benchmark for tracking visual states.
Even though video MLLMs can describe clips really well, they still cannot reliably track what changes over time.
This benchmark contains 834 videos and 1,500 questions where the answer cannot be found in a keyframe, with humans getting 90.5%, and Gemini 3.1 Pro gets only 44.4%.
The failure is mostly visual perception and not reasoning, because models solve the same tasks when the video events are written out in text.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Trust Region On-Policy Distillation”
On-policy distillation is powerful, but one bad mismatch between student and teacher can negatively impact the gradients.
So this paper's TrOPD only learns where the teacher is reliable, treats outliers separately, and nudges the student back onto teacher-like reasoning paths.
Providing much cleaner gradients and stabler long-CoT distillation.

summary:
"Self-Trained Verification for Training- and Test-Time Self-Improvement"
Reasoning models improve faster with a good verifier, but verifiers can't learn to catch subtle errors on their own.
However, a model that can't spot its own mistakes usually can when shown the correct answer.
This paper trains the verifier to imitate that "answer-in-hand" version of itself, then runs it without the answer at test time.
It roughly doubles accuracy on hard math and lifts science reasoning 14x. Training the generator against this verifier also pushes past where standard RL stalls.

On-policy distillation usually matches teacher and student only at the token probability level, throwing away the teacher’s hidden states.

“OrderGrad: Optimizing Beyond the Mean with Order-Statistic Policy Gradient Estimation”
Most RL optimizes average reward, but deployment often cares about the best sample, worst tail, median, CVaR, or shorter correct answers.
This paper makes policy gradients optimize sorted rewards directly, by weighting ranks instead of raw rewards.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“On the Geometry of On-Policy Distillation”
OPD is not just SFT mixed with RLVR. It has its own update geometry.
This paper shows that OPD updates fewer weights than SFT and preserves pretrained structure better, while staying less constrained than RLVR.
The key finding is subspace locking. OPD quickly settles into a small low-dimensional update channel, and restricting training to this early channel preserves performance.
So OPD is better understood as geometry-controlled distillation, not just dense teacher supervision on student rollouts.

clean_title: Trajectory-Refined Distillation improves supervision in on-policy learning
summary:
"Trajectory-Refined Distillation"
This paper shows a core failure in on-policy distillation.
When a student takes a wrong reasoning path, the teacher is forced to supervise from that broken prefix, so token-level KL becomes noisy.
So they introduced TRD that fixes this by refining the whole rollout first.
What it does is the teacher rewrites the student trajectory into a better reasoning path, then the student distills from that corrected trajectory.
While this is a small change, it still moves distillation from token fixes to trajectory fixes, giving cleaner supervision and stronger reasoning gains.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HKeSnNeW8AA4Sam.jpg
clean_summary: This work identifies a core failure in on-policy distillation: when a student makes a wrong reasoning path, the teacher's supervision becomes noisy because it is based on the broken prefix. To address this, TRD (Trajectory-Refined Distillation) is introduced, which refines the entire rollout before distillation. The teacher rewrites the student's trajectory into a better reasoning path, and the student then distills from this corrected trajectory. Although a small change, it shifts the focus from token-level fixes to trajectory-level fixes, resulting in cleaner supervision and stronger reasoning improvements.

This paper uses expressive flow policies for RL without making policy training fragile.

The key idea is to guide each denoising step with a critic gradient, but compute that gradient on an approximate clean action rather than a potential noisy intermediate action.

Training only the discovered sparse subnetwork nearly recovers the full OPD performance, indicating that OPD behaves more like sparse on-policy model editing than traditional supervised fine-tuning.

summary:
"Dynamic Linear Attention"
Most long context linear models compress tokens using fixed blocks or log schedules, but long text is not uniform. Stable spans can be summarized, while semantic shifts need higher resolution.
So this paper makes linear attention memory adaptive instead of fixed.
DLA uses a State Information Score to detect token level drift, creates new memory states at information transitions, and keeps a fixed cache by merging adjacent low information states.
The result is bounded cost with less irreversible information loss. Across Mamba 2 and Gated DeltaNet, DLA beats Log Linear Attention on commonsense, retrieval, RULER, and LongBench, while also improving throughput and memory.

The result is a method with bounded computational cost that retains more information, outperforming log-linear attention on benchmarks like Mamba 2, Gated DeltaNet, and others, while also improving throughput and memory efficiency.

The proposed Bebop which fixes it by using rejection sampling plus an end-to-end TV loss that directly trains MTP for target-draft overlap.

The proposed Bebop method addresses this by combining rejection sampling with an end-to-end total variation (TV) loss that directly trains MTP for target-draft overlap. clean_title: Temporal Difference in Vision: Learning from Video via Motion
summary:
Another interesting paper supervised by Yann LeCun!
"You Don't Need Strong Assumptions: Visual Representation Learning via Temporal Differences"
This paper proposes Temporal Difference in Vision (TDV), which is a simple idea for learning vision from video.
You basically don’t teach the model what to ignore with crops, masks, or augmentations, you simply teach it that the past becomes the future through motion.
So the model learns: current frame representation + motion representation = next frame representation
They demonstrated that strong assumptions help less as data grows, because TDV can already compete with DINO and iBOT on spatial and motion-heavy vision tasks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HK96CKYWoAAztgw.jpg
clean_summary:
Another interesting paper supervised by Yann LeCun. 'You Don't Need Strong Assumptions: Visual Representation Learning via Temporal Differences' introduces Temporal Difference in Vision (TDV), a simple idea for learning visual representations from video data.

Instead of relying on crops, masks, or augmentations to teach the model what to ignore, TDV teaches the model that the past becomes the future through motion. The model learns that current frame representation plus motion representation equals the next frame's representation.

Experiments show that as data increases, strong assumptions matter less because TDV already competes with methods like DINO and iBOT on tasks involving spatial and motion-heavy vision, demonstrating its effectiveness.

AI safety papers often say models are deceptive, scheming, or self-preserving, but many results only show behavior that looks human-like.

The key point is most scary L3 claims about intent or mechanisms are only backed by L1 behavioral evidence.

With how robot dexterity is bottlenecked by data as teleoperation and MoCap are expensive and internet videos are only observational, this paper turns normal RGB human videos into executable robot hand trajectories.
It reconstructs the hand and object, tracks the object with SAM 3D guided diffusion, then retargets the motion through physics-aware optimization so a real dexterous hand can do the same task.
The result is a path from internet video to real robot rollouts, with retargeting success improving from 25% to 71% on noisy reconstructions.

"How Transparent is DiffusionGemma?"
With how Diffusion LMs denoise tokens instead of generating from left to right, there's a concern about how reasoning will be hidden in the denoising steps.
But this paper shows DiffusionGemma is more readable than expected.
At first, it looks much more opaque than Gemma 4 because the model runs many denoising steps before reaching something we can clearly read. In the paper’s opaque serial depth metric, DiffusionGemma is 608,016 vs 21,235 for Gemma 4, which is where the 28.6x more opaque.
But once the denoising bottleneck is treated as readable by mapping hidden states into likely text tokens, DiffusionGemma drops to 23,571, only 1.1x Gemma 4.
What's also really cool is that it contains some diffusion-only behaviors. It can change earlier answers after later reasoning, guess response length early, write code skeleton-first, and keep multiple token possibilities alive before settling.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"VIMPO: Value-Implicit Policy Optimization for LLMs"
While GRPO is simple because it avoids a critic, it still gives every token in a reasoning trace the same reward signal.
This paper tries to get the best of both worlds by deriving the value function from the policy itself using policy-reference log-ratios, so the model gets token-level credit assignment without training a separate critic.
On math RLVR, VIMPO beats GRPO across MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, and OlympiadBench, and stays stronger under noisy rewards.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Sparrow: Sparse Rollout for Stable and Efficient Long-context RL of LLMs"
Long-context RLVR is powerful, but most of the cost comes from generating huge CoT rollouts.
Sparse attention would make this faster, it's just that the naive sparse rollouts would drift from the dense policy and can collapse training.
This paper finds that stability depends on the worst-aligned tail of tokens, not the average mismatch.
So by keeping the 5th percentile sparse-to-dense acceptance rate around 0.86 with dynamic sparsity, Sparrow gets about 2x rollout speedups while matching dense RL performance.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
TMax: An open RL recipe for terminal agents
I’m very excited to get to share a new RL paper today that I got to have a small part in – a type of paper I suspect we’ll see much more of in the future. The key is that RL research is very different today, in mid-2026, than what most observers have in their context. The average conception of an RL paper is grounded in the RLVR revolution of early 2025, where many people could use vanilla RLVR libraries to hillclimb on math benchmarks. Crucially, this style of math work could be done on base models or fairly stably on already trained models. With agents, the tasks of focus are very hard, requiring complex tool-use, harnesses where the model automatically manages its history, and much more training to make smaller eval improvements. We’re shifting from a renaissance of RL study to rapidly needing to improve its empirical rigor and common community engagements.
TMax is the best open data for hillclimbing on frontier terminal tasks. It’s been validated with rigorous experiments, and if the authors wanted to just form a “RL environments startup” they could probably sell it for millions of dollars. This data work is some of my favorite stuff to be around in my 2.5+ years at Ai2.
As a general summary, the recipe is open data and recipe lessons from hillclimbing the Qwen 3.5 smaller, dense models on terminal tasks. These models are super hard to hillclimb in this area, as they’re already trained heavily on the task. The training is very infrastructure-dependent, and most of the RL innovations are more designed to make training stable than to improve the rate of learning.
I strongly recommend this paper. I joke around that I was happy to be an author just so I had to read it twice! You can find Hamish’s thread sharing more here or read the paper here. You can click through to find the model weights, the data, and even some fun further artifacts to study like all the RL rollouts from a training run – where the model sometimes became aware that it was being tested.
The biggest takeaway I have from following this work, and more of the work in the community, is how important recipe work is. Let me define “recipe work.” It is a style of paper that explains all the steps you need to make crucial model improvements – data, algorithm, codebase, pitfalls, etc.
Getting started in meaningful RL experiments today is a substantial expense. There are a ton of companies, an entire industry emerging really, around the idea of taking open-weight language models and finetuning them with RL on your domain-specific tasks. What I see in many projects is that getting an initial baseline is very hard. This phase, which can cost weeks and anywhere from $10K to $1M+, feels like spinning your wheels (A fun fact is that an RL step on a model like Nvidia Nemotron 3 Ultra on Tinker costs $1K and a meaningful RL run would be hundreds of steps – credit Edward Hu). It takes a lot of time to get traction in learning signal on meaningful, hard RL tasks.
What we need as a community is a way for people to study small ablations to established RL recipes, as most labs won’t have the resources to do it from scratch in a meaningful way. This is what I hope TMAX can be for terminal agents, or the start of. Yes the training jobs are expensive, as the paper documents a standard training job being 8 nodes of H100s (2 train 6 inference) for 2-3 days, but that is approaching something academics can study. The establishment of this recipe took O(100) of these training jobs to get right.
This isn’t my first time trying to establish this direction. When we launched Olmo 3 we had the “RL Zero“ model families, which are clean RL runs from a base model on a certain domain. This type of recipe-dependent work is a clear indicator that meaningful post-training work today looks much more like pretraining work of years past. We need decision-making ladders, clear ways of seeing small improvements in the models, stability, and so on.
Part of this is down to academic gatekeepers, who won’t reward a paper doing very clean empirical work to push a recipe 1-2% up. They’ll favor a “new algorithm” that matches results, or something sort of bogus. My hope is that we can have multiple, stable, clear recipes across agent types, so innovations can be tested more clearly in multiple domains. (If you’re working on this, please reach out – I’m happy to support if I can, but I likely can’t reply to every email).
As a quick aside, the RL frameworks in vogue today seem to be SLIME and SkyRL. The libraries of choice have shifted throughout these seasons in RL, which further contributes to a form of fragility in the literature. A bit of continuity will go a long way.
So, go read this paper. It’s a really great example of how seemingly simple data and infrastructure work can be very hard and impactful. It’s also got me looking for more applications of Divergence Proximal Policy Optimization (DPPO) as another small evolution to the best RL algorithms of the day, by virtue of being a bit more stable by improving token-level clipping.

summary:
OCR but with a working memory...?!
This paper, Unlimited OCR, replaces decoder full self-attention with Reference Sliding Window Attention, giving the model a working memory where each token attends to the fixed visual and prompt references plus only the most recent output tokens, making decode KV cache constant instead of linear in generation length.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“Tapered Language Models”
Most LMs give every layer the same MLP width, but the paper shows this is probably wasteful.
Early layers seem to write more new information into the residual stream, while later layers mostly refine what is already there.
So instead of making the model bigger, they simply move MLP capacity forward. Early layers get wider FFNs, later layers get thinner FFNs, and the average width stays the same.
The best setup they found uses a smooth cosine taper from 1.5x normal MLP width in early layers to 0.5x in late layers, keeping total params and FLOPs fixed.
This improves perplexity and downstream accuracy across Transformers, Gated Attention, Hope-attention, and Titans.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLq27cFXgAAwjJZ.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Most model scores across benchmarks can be predicted from a few probe evals
summary:
You Don’t Need to Run Every Eval
LLM eval suites look like dozens of independent benchmarks, but this paper shows the public score matrix is basically rank-2.
That means most model scores across 133 benchmarks can be predicted from just a few probe evals.
This paper, BenchPress, uses low-rank matrix completion to recover missing scores within about 4.6 points, and five carefully chosen benchmarks can predict the rest of a scorecard within 3.93 points.
So evals may be less like running every test, and more like measuring the right few coordinates of model capability.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLrFDo3WwAAPNKm.jpg

If there's auto-research, shouldn't there also be a auto-data generation?
In this new Meta paper, they proposed Autodata, which makes synthetic data generation work more like a data scientist, with an agent that creates tasks, tests them on weak and strong models, studies what failed, and revises the data until it gives the target model a useful learning signal.
And it's not just about making harder data, it's data that is just right to learn from. In their experiment, a 4B model beat standard Self Instruct training and even outperform a larger 397B baseline on legal reasoning.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Training for the Model You Return"
Most LM pipelines return an EMA or averaged checkpoint, but optimizers still train like the final iterate is what matters.
So if the output is an averaged model, can we shape training so that average gets better?
This paper introduces PACE, a small AdamW wrapper that pulls weights toward their EMA during training, as EMA is not just post processing, it is the estimator. So training should optimize the whole trajectory, not only the endpoint.
This makes the averaged model itself better across 1 to 2B LM fine tuning and GPT 2 pretraining.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Sakana AI's Fugu: Dynamic multi-agent orchestration for diverse tasks
summary:
Sakana Fugu Technical Report
Instead of training one larger model, Sakana AI trains an orchestrator that reads each query and dynamically routes or composes GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Claude Opus 4.8 and other agents into query-specific workflows.
With Fugu being the fast router, and Fugu-Ultra being the deep multi-agent conductor, trained with SFT, evolutionary strategies and GRPO to build adaptive scaffolds.
The idea is to have the model pick GPT for math, Gemini for science and recall, Opus for debugging, then synthesize them when no single agent is best.
This router is able to get SoTA results across SWE-Bench Pro, Terminal Bench, LiveCodeBench, GPQA-Diamond, CharXiv and more, demonstrating the potential of orchestration being a practical alternative beyond training.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL10tBfXIAAxGRo.jpg
clean_summary:
Sakana AI trains an orchestrator that reads each query and dynamically routes or composes multiple agents like GPT-5.5, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Claude Opus 4.8 into task-specific workflows, instead of training a single large model.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Improved large language diffusion models with bidirectional masked diffusion
summary:
"Improved Large Language Diffusion Models"
ByteDance just made bidirectional masked diffusion on-par with autoregessive LM!
This paper iLLaDA trains an 8B Transformer from scratch on 12T tokens, then keeps the same denoising objective for SFT on a 25B-token instruction corpus.
It improves LLaDA with GQA, tied embeddings, variable-length generation, confidence-based MCQ scoring, and packed-sequence diffusion SFT.
iLLaDA-Base raises the average score from 51.1 to 63.9 and slightly exceeds Qwen2.5 7B Base at 63.3, while iLLaDA-Instruct still trails Qwen2.5 Instruct without RL alignment.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL10zyZWUAAQ4tc.jpg
clean_summary:
ByteDance has developed bidirectional masked diffusion models that match autoregressive language models in performance. The paper introduces iLLaDA, which trains an 8B Transformer on 12 trillion tokens and applies the same denoising objective for supervised fine-tuning on a 25B-token instruction dataset.

iLLaDA improves over LLaDA by incorporating techniques like GQA, tied embeddings, variable-length generation, confidence-based multiple-choice scoring, and packed-sequence diffusion supervised fine-tuning. The base model increases the average score from 51.1 to 63.9, slightly surpassing Qwen2.5 7B Base at 63.3, although the instruct version still trails Qwen2.5 Instruct without reinforcement learning alignment.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: SPIRAL: learning to search and aggregate for better reasoning scaling
summary:
"SPIRAL: Learning to Search and Aggregate"
This paper gets up to 11x better scaling efficiency by training the model to search and aggregate, not just think longer.
So most reasoning RL trains one chain of thought, but real test-time scaling uses many attempts plus a final synthesis step. This paper however trains that full pipeline end-to-end.
The key idea is set RL, where parallel traces get reward for being useful together, even if none of them solves the problem alone.
On math reasoning, SPIRAL beats GRPO by up to 15% when scaling search plus aggregation.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL6tjtFWsAA0pvH.jpg
clean_summary: SPIRAL is a method that achieves up to 11 times better scaling efficiency by training models to search and aggregate reasoning attempts, rather than just thinking longer. Unlike most reinforcement learning approaches that train a single chain of thought, SPIRAL trains the entire pipeline end-to-end, including multiple attempts and a final synthesis step. It uses set RL, where parallel traces are rewarded for being collectively useful, even if none individually solves the problem. On math reasoning tasks, SPIRAL outperforms GRPO by up to 15% when scaling search and aggregation.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: DeepSeek's DSpark improves throughput and efficiency with speculative decoding
summary:
DeepSeek just published DSpark, a speculative decoding system that boosts live DeepSeek V4 serving throughput by 51% to 406% under stricter latency targets.
With how most speculative decoding methods draft more tokens, but waste verification compute when those tokens get rejected, DSpark fixes this with a semi autoregressive drafter for more coherent long drafts, plus a confidence scheduler that only verifies prefixes likely to survive.
It also gives 60% to 85% faster per user generation at matched throughput.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL6tpMYW8AAGpxB.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Evaluating diverse memory systems for agent-native memory architectures
summary:
"Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System?"
Agents do not just need longer context windows. They need a real memory system, as agent memory now is more like a data management layer, not a retrieval problem.
This paper breaks memory into representation and storage, extraction, retrieval and routing, and maintenance, then evaluates 12 memory systems across 11 datasets.
They found that no memory architecture wins across the board. Graph memory is strong for updated facts and entity relations, hybrid systems do better for filtered recall, long context still helps when chronology matters, and append-only memory mostly returns facts.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL_3MmKXUAAdr0S.jpg
clean_summary:
Agents need more than longer context windows; they require a true memory system. This work breaks memory into components like representation, storage, extraction, retrieval, routing, and maintenance, then assesses 12 different memory architectures across 11 datasets.

The findings show that no single memory architecture dominates universally. Graph memory excels at handling updated facts and entity relations, hybrid systems perform better for filtered recall, long context remains useful when chronology is important, and append-only memory mainly stores facts. This highlights the complexity of designing effective memory systems for agents.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Decomposing LLM evaluation into atomic yes/no questions for better interpretability
summary:
Instead of asking an LLM judge for one broad score, this paper decomposes evaluation into many atomic yes or no questions that are easier to verify and debug.
This paper proposed a meta-prompt that turns the task requirements into fine-grained checks, then an evaluator answers each question independently and aggregates them into interpretable scores across dimensions like coherence, consistency, and relevance.
So evaluation doesn't just say an output is bad, it also reveals exactly which requirement failed and why.
Across SummEval, Topical-Chat and QAGS, BINEVAL matches or beats strong baselines like UniEval and G-Eval, with especially strong results on factual consistency and hallucination detection.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL_3UdZXcAAHAax.png
clean_summary: Instead of asking an LLM judge for a single broad score, this approach breaks down evaluation into many atomic yes or no questions that are easier to verify and debug. A meta-prompt converts task requirements into fine-grained checks, and an evaluator answers each question independently, then aggregates the answers into scores across dimensions like coherence, consistency, and relevance. This method not only indicates whether an output is bad but also explains which requirement failed and why. Experiments on SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS show that BINEVAL matches or outperforms strong baselines like UniEval and G-Eval, especially in factual consistency and hallucination detection.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: DiffusionBlocks potentially save 2-3x training memory, but sensitivity to training budget
summary:
DiffusionBlocks that can potentially save 2-3x training memory... Does it replicate?
We tested this on our latest AutoResearch tool that lets you replicate research in just a simple click.
With our small replication setup, we were able to learn that the method is training-budget sensitive. At only 25% of the required epochs, DiffusionBlocks had not yet caught up to the end-to-end baseline.
However, as we increased the amount of layers from 12 to 24 which the paper did not explore, DiffusionBlocks was able to beat the baseline with just 25% of the required epochs!
To top it all off, All of these experiments were done within 4 prompts:
- "Can you get a minimal reproduction of DiffusionBlocks running end to end?"
- "Can you do a 8 epochs and compare between block=2 and 3?"
- "Can you do a 24 layers with block = 2 vs 3?"
- "Can you do 12 and 24 layers with blocks=2 & 3, but this time with 24 epochs?"
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMGR6CcWkAAC_XW.jpg
clean_summary: DiffusionBlocks are a technique that could significantly reduce training memory usage, potentially by two to three times. Testing on an AutoResearch tool revealed that the method is sensitive to the training budget; at only 25% of the required epochs, it did not match the baseline. However, when increasing the number of layers from 12 to 24, which was not explored in the original paper, DiffusionBlocks was able to outperform the baseline with just 25% of the epochs. These experiments were conducted through simple prompts, including comparisons of layer blocks and epoch counts, demonstrating the method's potential when scaled appropriately.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Transformers attention heads can be replaced by synthesized Python programs
summary:
Explaining attention heads by turning them into... Python code?
So for each head, they record its attention maps, then use another LM to synthesize a program that predicts the same token-to-token attention pattern from the input text.
And this code can replace the real attention heads inside the model.
On GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Llama-3B, the best programs match real attention with 69%, 74%, and 79% mean IoU. Up to 30 to 40% of heads can be replaced before QA performance meaningfully drops.
Showing that many Transformer attention heads are not just neural black boxes. They actually behave like simple symbolic routines that can be written, tested, and swapped into the model.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMHzAFzWMAATJdb.jpg
clean_summary: Explaining attention heads by turning them into Python code involves recording each head's attention maps and using another language model to synthesize a program that predicts the same token-to-token attention pattern from the input text. This code can replace the actual attention heads within the model. On GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Llama-3B, the best programs achieve 69%, 74%, and 79% mean IoU with real attention. Replacing up to 30 to 40% of heads does not significantly impact question-answering performance, showing that many Transformer attention heads are not just neural black boxes but behave like simple symbolic routines that can be written, tested, and swapped into the model.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"HydraHead: From Head-Level Functional Heterogeneity to Specialized Attention Hybridization"
This paper shows that the right unit for hybrid attention is the head, not the layer.
So you have a few retrieval-critical heads to keep Full Attention, while the rest switch to Gated DeltaNet Linear Attention. The FA heads are chosen with causal patching, then FA and LA outputs are fused with scale normalization.
This gives a 7 to 1 LA to FA model that matches a heavier 3 to 1 layer-wise hybrid, which improves 512K retrieval by over 69% with only 15B training tokens, and preserves reasoning.
Another important insight here is that they turned interpretability from an analysis tool into an architecture design tool.
As they didn't just use causal analysis to explain what heads do, it also uses that analysis to decide which heads deserve Full Attention and which can be replaced with Linear Attention for efficient 512K-context scaling.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMHzIHaXgAASmgB.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Scaling models by their ability to act reliably rather than size
summary:
Scale by how long and reliably a model can act, not by simply making the model bigger.
This 35B MoE agent called Agents A1 reaches trillion parameter level performance by training on 45K token trajectories where knowledge, actions, tool outputs, failures, and verifier signals are linked into a Knowledge Action Graph.
Then it combines full domain SFT, specialized domain teachers, and domain routed on policy distillation with salient vocabulary alignment.
This approach beats or matches 1T models on several agentic benchmarks including SEAL 0, IFBench, HiPhO, FrontierScience Olympiad, and MolBench Bind.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMKwvZ6WoAAnu2G.jpg

A 35B MoE agent called Agents A1 achieves trillion-parameter-level performance by training on 45,000 token trajectories that link knowledge, actions, tool outputs, failures, and verifier signals into a Knowledge Action Graph. title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Orca: learning a unified world latent from video and language for diverse readouts
summary:
Next state prediction instead of next token, frame or action.
This paper, Orca, learns a unified world latent from video and language, then freezes the backbone and reads that latent into text, images, and robot actions.
The "unconscious learning" captures dense physical transitions from continuous video, while the "conscious learning" uses event captions and VQA to model sparse meaningful transitions.
Trained on 125K hours of video and 160M event annotations, Orca shows that stronger world latents improve all three readouts and can even boost robot action generation without action labels during pretraining.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMKw334XUAApLBc.jpg

Next state prediction instead of next token, frame, or action. Orca learns a unified world latent from video and language, then uses it to generate text, images, and robot actions.

It captures dense physical transitions from continuous video through 'unconscious learning' and models sparse meaningful transitions with event captions and VQA via 'conscious learning.' Trained on 125,000 hours of video and 160 million annotations, Orca demonstrates that stronger world latents enhance all three readouts and can even improve robot action generation without action labels during pretraining.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: AdaJEPA: test-time adaptation for world models using MPC and self-supervised learning
summary:
Yet another paper supervised by Yann LeCun: Test-time adaptation instead of frozen world models!?
This paper, AdaJEPA, takes a pretrained JEPA world model, plans with MPC, executes an action, then uses the observed transition to update the latent predictor before replanning.
The core loop is plan, act, adapt, replan. Every action creates its own self-supervised training signal through latent next-state prediction error.
With just one gradient step per MPC step, AdaJEPA improves goal-reaching under unseen shapes, visual corruptions, dynamics shifts, and new maze layouts.
The big idea they suggest is that world models should not stop learning after pretraining. They should keep recalibrating during deployment, turning real interaction into continual model correction.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPjVuTW4AAJMFo.jpg
clean_summary: This work builds on Yann LeCun's supervision approach by proposing AdaJEPA, which updates a pretrained JEPA world model during deployment. It plans with MPC, executes actions, and then uses the observed transitions to update the latent predictor before replanning. The core loop is plan, act, adapt, replan, with each action generating a self-supervised training signal through latent next-state prediction error. With just one gradient step per MPC cycle, AdaJEPA improves goal-reaching in unseen shapes, visual corruptions, dynamics shifts, and new maze layouts. The key idea is that world models should continue learning during deployment, turning real interactions into ongoing model correction.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Token-level routing in on-policy distillation to address privilege illusion
summary:
What if we have token-level routing instead of blindly distilling every token?
This paper, DOPD, fixes on-policy distillation when privileged hints or visual annotations make the teacher look stronger than it really is.
They identified the key problem being privilege illusion, where the teacher-student gap mixes true capability gap with an information gap the student cannot reproduce at inference.
DOPD compares privileged teacher and privileged student probabilities per token, then sends each token to the right objective. High-gap teacher-confident tokens get strong full-vocab JS distillation, while low-gap or uncertain tokens get lighter teacher signals or self-regularization.
Across Qwen3 and Qwen3-VL, DOPD beats vanilla OPD and strong baselines, with better stability, less entropy collapse, stronger scaling across model sizes, and better continual and out-of-distribution generalization.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMPjfb_WYAApsWk.jpg
clean_summary:
What if we have token-level routing instead of blindly distilling every token? The DOPD method fixes on-policy distillation when privileged hints or visual annotations make the teacher look stronger than it really is. It identifies the privilege illusion, where the gap between teacher and student combines true capability differences with an information gap the student cannot reproduce at inference.

DOPD compares privileged teacher and student probabilities per token, then assigns each token to the appropriate objective. Tokens with high teacher confidence receive full-vocab JS distillation, while uncertain tokens get lighter signals or self-regularization. Experiments on Qwen3 and Qwen3-VL show that DOPD outperforms vanilla OPD and other strong baselines, with improved stability, less entropy collapse, better scaling, and enhanced generalization to out-of-distribution data.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
clean_title: Rethinking reward design for robot policies: avoid collapsing multiple axes into a single score
summary:
We should stop optimizing robot policies against a single overall reward. Trajectories differ along many axes, such as speed, precision, and subtask completion, and one can be better on some while worse on others. If we collapse all of that into a single overall axis we lose this structure making the reward ambiguous and harder to optimize.

When all these aspects are combined into one reward, it makes the reward ambiguous and harder to optimize, losing the structure that distinguishes different qualities of behavior.

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
“LeVLJEPA”
Most vision-language models are trained with contrastive learning, where the model learns by comparing correct image-text pairs against incorrect ones.
This paper shows you can train vision-language models without those negative pairs. LeVLJEPA learns by making image embeddings predict text embeddings and text embeddings predict image embeddings, while SIGReg prevents the representations from collapsing.
It is worse than CLIP-style models for zero-shot classification, but better when the visual backbone needs strong patch-level features.
As a frozen backbone, it beats CLIP and SigLIP on segmentation, GQA, VQAv2, and POPE across two LLMs.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMTy_4OWkAE__OP.jpg

title: alphaXiv (@askalphaxiv)
summary:
"Bridging Spherical Black-Box Optimizers"
Black-box optimization is used when you can test solutions but cannot use gradients.
This paper shows that major methods like ES, OVI, CBO, pCBO, cCBO, and Diffusion Evolution can be written under one shared update rule.
The key difference is whether the optimizer prefers sharp or flat solutions, and whether it searches for one solution or multiple solutions.
Using this, the paper builds hybrid optimizers that are better for RL tasks and model merging when evaluations are expensive.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HMTzFZEW4AAkFJ_.jpg
